newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Libya violated flight ban - U.N. Security Council.
newsitem.headline: Libya violated flight ban - U.N. Security Council.

text.p: The U.N. Security Council mildly rebuked Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi on Tuesday for violating international sanctions by flying to Niger and Nigeria earlier this month.

In a statement, the council said it "takes note with concern" of reports that four Libyan-registered aircraft flew to Niger on May 8 and returned to Libya from Nigeria on May 10 in violation of air sanctions.
The council said its Libya sanctions committee would follow up the issue directly in talks with envoys from Libya, Niger and Nigeria.
The mildly worded statement was a compromise between the United States and Egypt, but Western diplomats said they were satisfied that the flights had been deemed a violation.
Libya said Gaddafi visited the West African countries to hold prayers marking the Moslem New Year as head of the Islamic Popular Leadership, a group he created in 1989.

Libya has been subject to mandatory U.N. sanctions since 1992, including a ban on international flights and an arms embargo, for failing to extradite two men wanted by Britain and the United States. They are suspects in the 1988 midair bombing of a Pan Am airliner over Lockerbie, Scotland, which killed 270 people.

Several countries said Libya's flights this month were for religious purposes and should be allowed, even though Libya had not sought permission in advance. Their position indicated that support would be weak for any further tightening of sanctions.

On Monday a bipartisan group of 53 senators sent a letter to Bill Richardson, the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, urging Washington to introduce a resolution to impose an oil embargo on Libya. But diplomats said chances of its passage would be remote, since previous U.S. attempts had failed almost before they began.
Libya was rapped on April 4 by the Security Council for flying pilgrims from Libya to Saudi Arabia.

It was the third consecutive year Libya had violated sanctions by flying pilgrims to Jeddah on an unauthorised flight, even though the council had given permission for an Egyptian airline to ferry Libyans wishing to make the annual pilgrimage to Mecca.

A second reason for the imposition of sanctions on Libya in 1992 was to penalise it for not cooperating in the investigation of the bombing of a French UTA airliner over Niger in 1989 that killed all 171 people aboard.

The curbs were toughened in 1993 to include a freeze on some of Libya's assets abroad and a ban on its import of certain types of equipment used in oil terminals and refineries. They do not affect the export of oil from Libya or its purchase of oil-drilling equipment.

The Organisation of African Unity and the Arab League recently told the Security Council that Libya had fully met its demands. They said that while Libya was unable to extradite the two Lockerbie suspects to Britain or the United States for trial, it was willing for them to be tried in a neutral country to be determined by the Security Council.
